Safety & Handling: Extreme radiation hazard. Mendelevium isotopes have relatively short half-lives (up to 51 days) and undergo spontaneous fission. It is handled exclusively in highly specialized particle accelerator facilities.

name: Nobelium
description:
Nobelium is a highly radioactive synthetic metal named after Alfred Nobel, the inventor of dynamite and founder of the Nobel Prize.

Lab Notes: Unusually for the later actinides, liquid-phase tracer chemistry has proven that the +2 oxidation state is actually the most stable state for nobelium in an aqueous solution, unlike most other actinides which strongly prefer the +3 state. This is because nobelium achieves a fully filled f-orbital configuration (5f14) when it loses two electrons, giving it unique stability.

Safety & Handling: Extreme radiation hazard. It is produced by bombarding curium or californium targets with carbon ions. With its longest-lived isotope having a half-life of just 58 minutes, it vanishes almost as quickly as it is created.

name: Lawrencium
description:
Lawrencium is a highly radioactive synthetic metal and is officially the final element of the actinide series. It was named after Ernest O. Lawrence, the inventor of the cyclotron (the first modern particle accelerator).

Lab Notes: Completing the 5f electron shell, lawrencium behaves exactly as expected for the final actinide, strongly favoring the +3 oxidation state. Its chemistry is notoriously difficult to study because it is synthesized one atom at a time and its longest-lived isotope survives for only about 11 hours. 

Safety & Handling: Extreme radiation hazard. Like its predecessors, it is never handled in bulk and exists entirely within the shielded, high-energy detection chambers of advanced physics laboratories.

name: Rutherfordium
description:
Rutherfordium is a highly radioactive synthetic metal. Its creation marked a monumental scientific milestone as the very first 'Transactinide' or 'Superheavy Element', officially starting the d-block of the 7th row of the periodic table.

Lab Notes: It is named after Ernest Rutherford, the father of nuclear physics. In ultra-fast radiochemical experiments, rutherfordium behaves similarly to hafnium and zirconium, forming stable +4 compounds (like RfCl4) that can be isolated as a gas for mere seconds before radioactive decay destroys the atoms entirely.

Safety & Handling: Extreme radiation hazard. It possesses no stable or naturally occurring isotopes. It decays via spontaneous fission and alpha emission in a matter of minutes or seconds.

name: Dubnium
description:
Dubnium is a highly radioactive, synthetic superheavy element. It is named after the town of Dubna in Russia, the home of the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research (JINR) where many superheavy elements were discovered.

Lab Notes: Based on periodic trends, dubnium should behave similarly to tantalum. However, due to extreme relativistic effects (where inner electrons orbit the heavy nucleus at near light-speed, warping the atom's chemical behavior), dubnium often behaves more like niobium. Chemical experiments must be performed via automated gas chromatography in seconds before the element disintegrates.

Safety & Handling: Extreme radiation hazard. With an incredibly brief half-life, dubnium presents zero biological risk outside of the specialized particle accelerators where it is momentarily forced into existence.

name: Seaborgium
description:
Seaborgium is a radioactive synthetic transactinide metal. It is highly famous because it was the first element ever named after a living person: the legendary nuclear chemist Glenn T. Seaborg, who was instrumental in synthesizing numerous transuranic elements.

Lab Notes: Sitting directly below tungsten in Group 6, seaborgium behaves exactly as predicted. Despite its most stable isotope lasting only a few minutes, chemists have successfully created seaborgium hexacarbonyl (Sg(CO)6), proving it forms transition metal complexes identically to tungsten and molybdenum.

Safety & Handling: Extreme radiation hazard. Created by smashing high-energy oxygen or neon ions into heavy actinide targets, it exists only fleetingly in heavy-ion accelerators.

name: Bohrium
description:
Bohrium is a superheavy, highly radioactive synthetic metal named in honor of the legendary Danish physicist Niels Bohr, whose model of the atom revolutionized quantum mechanics.

Lab Notes: Placed squarely in Group 7 beneath rhenium, bohrium is expected to be a dense transition metal. Gas-phase radiochemistry experiments have successfully synthesized bohrium oxychloride (BhO3Cl), confirming it exhibits the maximum +7 oxidation state characteristic of its group. It is produced by bombarding bismuth targets with massive chromium ions.

Safety & Handling: Extreme radiation hazard. Its longest-lived confirmed isotope has a half-life of barely 61 seconds. It rapidly decays via alpha emission and presents a hazard only to the highly specialized physicists creating it.

name: Hassium
description:
Hassium is a superheavy synthetic transition metal. It is named after the German state of Hesse, where the GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research (the facility that discovered it) is located.

Lab Notes: In one of the most stunning feats of microchemistry, scientists managed to react hassium atoms with oxygen to form hassium tetroxide (HsO4). This compound is highly volatile and behaves almost exactly like osmium tetroxide, beautifully confirming its placement in Group 8 of the periodic table despite the extreme relativistic effects warping its electron cloud.

Safety & Handling: Extreme radiation hazard. Hassium's most stable known isotopes have half-lives of less than ten seconds, decaying violently via alpha emission or spontaneous fission.

name: Meitnerium
description:
Meitnerium is a superheavy, radioactive synthetic metal. It was named in honor of Lise Meitner, the pioneering Austrian-Swedish physicist who theoretically explained and co-discovered nuclear fission.

Lab Notes: Meitnerium marks the boundary where chemical experiments become nearly impossible. Its half-life is measured in milliseconds, meaning it decays before any traditional or even ultra-fast gas-phase chemistry can be performed. Its properties are entirely extrapolated mathematically; it is predicted to be an incredibly dense noble metal similar to iridium.

Safety & Handling: Extreme radiation hazard. Due to its existence lasting mere fractions of a second, it poses no environmental or biological threat, existing only as transient data spikes on particle detectors.

name: Darmstadtium
description:
Darmstadtium is a highly radioactive synthetic transactinide metal. It was named after the city of Darmstadt, Germany, acknowledging the massive contributions of the GSI heavy-ion research facility to the discovery of superheavy elements.

Lab Notes: Sitting below platinum in Group 10, darmstadtium is predicted to be an incredibly dense, solid noble metal. However, like meitnerium, its half-life is far too short (roughly 10 seconds for its most stable isotope, and microseconds for others) to perform any chemical studies. It is strictly created atom by atom via 'cold fusion' pathways, bombarding lead targets with nickel ions.

Safety & Handling: Extreme radiation hazard. It undergoes violent alpha decay and spontaneous fission almost instantly upon creation, requiring massive arrays of magnetic separators and silicon detectors to even prove it existed.

name: Roentgenium
description:
Roentgenium is a highly radioactive synthetic superheavy metal. It is named in honor of Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen, the physicist who discovered X-rays.

Lab Notes: Sitting directly below gold in Group 11, it is predicted to be a highly noble metal. However, due to its incredibly short half-life (a few seconds for its most stable isotope), no chemical experiments have ever been successfully performed on it. Theoretical calculations suggest that relativistic effects would make it even less reactive than gold, potentially making it the most 'noble' of all metals.

Safety & Handling: Extreme radiation hazard. Roentgenium decays almost instantly via spontaneous fission or alpha emission. It poses zero environmental hazard as it exists only fleetingly within particle accelerator detection grids.

name: Copernicium
description:
Copernicium is a highly radioactive synthetic superheavy element. It is named after the legendary Renaissance astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus, who formulated the heliocentric model of the universe.

Lab Notes: Located beneath mercury, copernicium is an incredibly fascinating target for theoretical chemists. Advanced relativistic models predict that its valence electrons are drawn so tightly to the massive nucleus that it might actually behave more like a noble gas than a metal. Experiments attempting to measure its volatility suggest it is indeed highly volatile and might even be a gas at standard room temperature, though it is usually classified theoretically as a solid or liquid.

Safety & Handling: Extreme radiation hazard. Like its neighbors, it decays in seconds or fractions of a second and is handled entirely through automated detector arrays.

name: Nihonium
description:
Nihonium is a synthetic, highly radioactive superheavy metal. It holds the historical distinction of being the first element to be discovered in an Asian country, named after 'Nihon', the Japanese word for Japan.

Lab Notes: It is placed in Group 13 beneath thallium. While it is expected to share some metallic properties with its group members, relativistic effects are predicted to make the +1 oxidation state much more stable than the +3 state. It was synthesized by the RIKEN institute by cold-fusing bismuth targets with high-energy zinc ions.

Safety & Handling: Extreme radiation hazard. With a half-life of roughly 10 seconds for its most stable isotope, it decays violently and exists solely as a subject of heavy-ion physics research.

name: Flerovium
description:
Flerovium is a superheavy, radioactive synthetic metal. It is named after the Flerov Laboratory of Nuclear Reactions in Russia, a global leader in the discovery of superheavy elements.

Lab Notes: Flerovium is of massive interest to physicists because it lies near the predicted 'Island of Stability'—a theoretical region of the periodic table where superheavy isotopes might have exceptionally long half-lives. While current isotopes only last a few seconds, chemical experiments utilizing thermochromatography suggest flerovium is a highly volatile metal, potentially even a gas at room temperature, behaving somewhat similarly to noble gases.

Safety & Handling: Extreme radiation hazard. Produced by bombarding plutonium targets with calcium-48 beams, it undergoes spontaneous fission almost immediately upon formation.

name: Moscovium
description:
Moscovium is a highly radioactive synthetic element. It was named after the Moscow region, honoring the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research (JINR) located in Dubna.

Lab Notes: Sitting directly below bismuth in Group 15, moscovium is predicted to be a solid metal. Due to its incredibly short half-life (measured in milliseconds), macroscopic chemical studies are impossible. Theoretical physics predicts that due to strong spin-orbit coupling, it would behave chemically more like an alkali metal (favoring a +1 oxidation state) than a typical Group 15 element.

Safety & Handling: Extreme radiation hazard. It is synthesized by slamming an intense beam of calcium-48 ions into a target of radioactive americium. It is completely destroyed by alpha decay before it can ever leave the vacuum chamber.

name: Livermorium
description:
Livermorium is a synthetic, highly radioactive superheavy element. It is named in honor of the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in California, which heavily collaborated with Russian scientists to discover it.

Lab Notes: Placed in Group 16 below polonium, livermorium is predicted to be a solid post-transition metal. Its most stable isotope has a half-life of roughly 60 milliseconds. It is created via the hot fusion of curium and calcium atoms. If enough could ever be gathered, theoretical calculations suggest it would favor the +2 oxidation state, unlike the lighter chalcogens.

Safety & Handling: Extreme radiation hazard. Livermorium presents no biological risk as its ultra-short half-life means it decays back into lighter, slightly more stable superheavy elements almost at the exact moment of its creation.

name: Tennessine
description:
Tennessine is a highly radioactive synthetic superheavy element. It is named after the state of Tennessee to honor the contributions of the Oak Ridge National Laboratory in producing the rare actinide targets required for its synthesis.

Lab Notes: Although it is officially placed in Group 17 (the halogens), relativistic effects are predicted to warp its properties so heavily that it would not behave like a standard halogen at all. Instead of a volatile nonmetal or metalloid, tennessine is predicted to be a volatile solid post-transition metal that does not form diatomic molecules or standard anions.

Safety & Handling: Extreme radiation hazard. Synthesizing tennessine requires bombarding a highly radioactive berkelium target with calcium ions for months on end to yield just a handful of atoms, which then decay in milliseconds.

name: Oganesson
description:
Oganesson is the heaviest and final element currently known on the periodic table. It is incredibly unique for being named after a living person—Yuri Oganessian, the brilliant physicist who pioneered the 'cold fusion' pathways used to discover superheavy elements.

Lab Notes: Sitting at the very bottom of the noble gases (Group 18), oganesson shatters periodic trends. Due to immense relativistic effects, its electron shells are predicted to lose their distinct structure and smear into a 'Fermi gas'. Consequently, it is predicted to be highly reactive (not noble at all) and would exist as a solid metal at room temperature, rather than a gas.

Safety & Handling: Extreme radiation hazard. Only a few atoms of Oganesson have ever been successfully synthesized. It decays in less than a millisecond via alpha emission, making it one of the most fleeting and mysterious substances in the known universe.
